claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of atomic or chemical disorder.
Atomic disorder modulates electron-scattering rates.
Disorder-induced changes in electron-phonon coupling control the superconducting critical temperature.
The initial HEA is produced by equiatomic mixing.
The initial HEA has a high degree of atomic disorder.
Thermal annealing can promote partial atomic ordering while preserving overall composition.
Variations in local atomic arrangement produce changes in electron-scattering rates.
Variations in local atomic arrangement produce changes in the local electronic density of states.
Increased disorder enhances electron scattering.
Disorder can modify electron-phonon coupling.
Disorder-favored localized vibrational modes can strengthen superconducting pairing interactions.
Strengthening pairing through localized vibrational modes may increase Tc.
Excessive disorder can disrupt coherent pairing and lower Tc.
Annealing-induced reduction of disorder is expected to alter electron scattering, electron-phonon interactions, and superconducting pairing.
Relative to the as-cast state, the less-disordered annealed sample should show a measurable shift in Tc.
Relative to the as-cast state, the less-disordered annealed sample should show a modified superconducting gap structure.
The direction of the Tc shift depends on whether disorder enhances pairing or suppresses coherence.
The proposed mechanism applies only when composition is constant and configurational disorder is the primary changed variable.
Additional impurities or drastic composition changes may place the material outside the proposed mechanism's domain.
An absence of any statistically significant and reproducible change in both Tc and superconducting gap structure after verified disorder reduction would falsify the hypothesis.
